source.title: The Scaling Law in Stellar Light Curves
source.authors: Jia-Shu Pan; Yuan-Sen Ting; Yang Huang; Jie Yu; Ji-Feng Liu

record.file_problem: The opening is garbled or displaced: the abstract begins with a citation fragment and introductory text. The paper otherwise appears to run through the references.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports scaling results in stellar light curves, a non-text time-series domain, and describes loss curves becoming shallower after a data-limited critical point. This refines the scope of a single power-law account.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling work as background, but those cited results are not recorded here. It reports its own compute- and parameter-scaling results using stellar light curves. Architecture variants are described, but no fixed-parameter comparison quantifying the effect of depth, width, or other architecture details is reported.
record.test_reason: The study trains GPT-2-like models from scratch (10^4 to 1.5B parameters) on Kepler stellar light curves. It fits its own power laws: test Huber loss against compute (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2) and downstream log g MSE against parameters (Sec. 4.2, Fig. 4). This is a new, non-text setting with results on the claim, so T3 rather than T5. The paper does not argue that any version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that GPT-2-like models trained on stellar light curves show a scaling law in next-token Huber loss versus compute, with no plateau up to 1.5B parameters. The downstream log g MSE also follows a power law in parameters, mirroring pretraining loss. Pretrained representations are 3 to 10 times more label-efficient than supervised Astroconformer. They attribute the shallow slope to the fixed 0.7B-token dataset, call for a training-set-size ablation, and extrapolate gains at larger compute.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GPT-2-like autoregressive models on continuous stellar light curves, with Huber loss for next-step regression rather than language-model cross-entropy. The compute sweep is evaluated at critical points; training data size is fixed.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that test-loss curves become shallower after the 3.4-epoch critical point, and suspects the fixed, limited training-data size as the cause.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed precision, GPT-2 XL representations need 3 to 10 times fewer labeled samples than the supervised Astroconformer (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaled self-supervised pretraining improves label efficiency on downstream tasks relative to supervised baselines.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: The pretraining scaling experiment uses a fixed training dataset of 0.7B tokens, and the authors identify limited data as a possible bottleneck. The reported scaling fits have no uncertainty estimates in the text. The compute-loss curve becomes shallower after the critical point.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out.

untested.parts: Not tested: no language-model cross-entropy. Huber loss on light curves is covered under V5.
The paper extrapolates (3.8% loss gain at 10^4 PF-days; 11%/23% lower log g MSE at 10B/100B parameters) but never checks these against larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation sweep; training data is fixed at 0.7B tokens.
Depth, heads and width are varied only to change size. There is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Data/token scaling, repeated-data laws, and fine-tuning or transfer scaling laws are not tested.
Only one downstream task (log g regression) with a frozen-probe protocol; no text tasks.
No comparison of fitting choices, schedules or setups. The definition-dependent critical point is not varied.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T3: the paper is a new-domain replication, not an argument against a version. V7 was removed from r1 and r2, and the V7 'supports' label was dropped. The post-critical-point bend comes from the authors' own truncation and critical-point definition in a data-limited, multi-epoch regime; it is not a demonstration of fit-dependence. All fits lack uncertainty and goodness-of-fit, and the loss range in Fig. 2 is narrow (about 4.05e-3 to 4.4e-3). Peer reviewed at ICML 2024.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses astronomical time series rather than language models and reports Huber loss, not held-out language-model cross-entropy.
It extrapolates from its fits, but does not validate predictions against substantially larger held-out runs.
No loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation sweep at fixed compute is reported.
Although model depth, head count, and width are varied, the paper does not report a controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests stellar light-curve time series with fixed training data; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as distinct training regimes.
It measures downstream surface-gravity inference versus parameter count, but does not establish a general downstream relationship across tasks or model families.
It reports loss curves becoming shallower after a critical point, but does not compare fitted exponents across setups or fitting methods, or examine compute-optimal allocation.

rows.subject: GPT-2-like models (aggregate across the tested model sizes)
rows.size_stated: Models span 10^4–10^9 parameters; largest trained model is approximately 1.5B parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Fit test-set next-token prediction Huber loss at critical points as a function of compute budget.
rows.measure: Test-set next-token prediction Huber loss versus compute budget
rows.note: The fit is reported at the critical points of the test-loss curves. The paper says a tenfold larger compute budget corresponds to a 1% improvement in next-token Huber loss.
rows.check: Not V7: one fit, with no comparison of setups or fitting methods. The fit is a power law over roughly six decades of compute (10^-5 to 10^1 PF-days). The exponent is very shallow (alpha_C = -0.00448, about 1% gain per tenfold compute). The fit uses each curve's loss at the 3.4-epoch 'critical point', which the authors chose as where curves fall below the trend. No uncertainty or fit quality is given.

conditions.value: Kepler stellar light curves; fixed training dataset of 0.7B tokens
3.4 epochs; curves after this point are shown as translucent

rows.measure: Test-set next-token prediction Huber loss versus compute; curve slope after the critical point
rows.baseline: Overall scaling law fitted at critical points
rows.value: After the critical point, the local slope becomes shallower than the overall scaling law; loss plateaus at lower values for larger models.
rows.note: The authors suspect the shallower slope is due to limited training data. This describes a departure from the fitted trend later in training.
rows.check: This describes how the critical point and truncation are defined, not an independent test. The authors define the critical point as where the local slope falls below the overall law, so the 'bend' is partly built into the method. The bend occurs in a multi-epoch (11.4 epochs), fixed-data (0.7B tokens) regime that the authors attribute to limited data. V1/V3-style laws exclude data-bottlenecked regimes, and no alternative fits are compared, so this is not evidence for V7 fit-dependence. Remove V7.
